In [[algebraic geometry]], the '''Iitaka dimension''' of a [[line bundle]] ''L'' on an [[algebraic variety]] ''X'' is the dimension of the image of the [[rational map]] to [[projective space]] determined by ''L''. This is 1 less than the dimension of the [[section ring]] of ''L''
:<math>R(X, L) = \bigoplus_{d=0}^\infty H^0(X, L^{\otimes d}).</math>
The Iitaka dimension of ''L'' is always less than or equal to the dimension of ''X''. If ''L'' is not effective, then its Iitaka dimension is usually defined to be <math>-\infty</math> or simply said to be negative (some early references define it to be &minus;1).  The Iitaka dimension of ''L'' is sometimes called L-dimension, while the dimension of a divisor D is called D-dimension. The Iitaka dimension was introduced by {{harvs|txt|first= Shigeru|last=Iitaka|authorlink= Shigeru Iitaka|year1=1970|year2=1971}}.

==Big line bundles==
A [[line bundle]] is '''big''' if it is of maximal Iitaka dimension, that is, if its Iitaka dimension is equal to the dimension of the underlying variety. Bigness is a [[birational geometry|birational]] invariant: If {{nowrap|''f'' : ''Y'' &rarr; ''X''}} is a birational morphism of varieties, and if ''L'' is a big line bundle on ''X'', then ''f''<sup>*</sup>''L'' is a big line bundle on ''Y''.

All [[ample line bundle]]s are big.

Big line bundles need not determine birational isomorphisms of ''X'' with its image.  For example, if ''C'' is a [[hyperelliptic curve]] (such as a curve of genus two), then its [[canonical bundle]] is big, but the rational map it determines is not a birational isomorphism.  Instead, it is a two-to-one cover of the [[canonical curve]] of ''C'', which is a [[rational normal curve]].

==Kodaira dimension==
{{main|Kodaira dimension}}
The Iitaka dimension of the canonical bundle of a [[smooth variety]] is called its [[Kodaira dimension]].

== Iitaka conjecture ==
[[File:M-pluricanonical map of complex manifolds M to W.svg|thumb|upright=0.72|The m-pluricanonical map of complex manifolds ''M'' to ''W'' induces a fiber space structure.]]

Consider on complex algebraic varieties in the following.

Let K be the [[canonical bundle]] on M. The dimension of H<sup>0</sup>(M,K<sup>m</sup>), holomorphic sections of K<sup>m</sup>, is denoted by P<sub>m</sub>(M), called '''m-genus'''. Let
::<math>N(M)=\{m\ge1|P_m(M)\ge1\},</math>
then N(M) becomes to be all of the positive integer with non-zero m-genus. When N(M) is not empty, for <math>m\in N(M)</math> [[Kodaira dimension#The plurigenera|m-pluricanonical map]] <math>\Phi_{mK}</math> is defined as the map
:<math>\begin{align}
\Phi_{mK}: & M\longrightarrow\ \ \ \ \ \ \mathbb{P}^N \\
& z\ \ \ \mapsto\ \ (\varphi_0(z):\varphi_1(z):\cdots:\varphi_N(z)) 
\end{align}</math>
where <math>\varphi_i</math> are the bases of H<sup>0</sup>(M,K<sup>m</sup>). Then the image of <math>\Phi_{mK}</math>, <math>\Phi_{mK}(M)</math> is defined as the submanifold of <math>\mathbb{P}^N</math>.

For certain <math>m</math> let <math>\Phi_{mk}:M\rightarrow W=\Phi_{mK}(M)\subset \mathbb{P}^N</math> be the m-pluricanonical map where W is the [[complex manifold]] embedded into projective space '''P'''<sup>N</sup>.

In the case of surfaces with κ(M)=1 the above W is replaced by a curve C, which is an elliptic curve (κ(C)=0). We want to extend this fact to the general dimension and obtain the analytic fiber structure depicted in the upper right figure.

[[File:M-pluricanonical map that is birational invariant.png|thumb|240px|left|The m-pluricanonical map is birational invariant. P<sub>m</sub>(M)=P<sub>m</sub>(W)]]

Given a birational map <math>\varphi:M \longrightarrow W</math>, m-pluricanonical map brings the commutative diagram depicted in the left figure, which means that <math>\Phi_{mK}(M)=\Phi_{mK}(W)</math>, i.e. m-pluricanonical genus is birationally invariant.

[[File:Existence of the birational map in the projective space.png|thumb|240px|The existence of the birational map ψ : 
W<sub>m1</sub> → W<sub>m2</sub> in the projective space ]]

It is shown by Iitaka that given n-dimensional compact complex manifold ''M'' with its Kodaira dimension κ(M) satisfying 1 ≤ κ(M) ≤ n-1, there are enough large ''m''<sub>1</sub>,''m''<sub>2</sub> such that <math>\Phi_{m_1K}:M\longrightarrow W_{m_1}(M)</math> and <math>\Phi_{m_2K}:M\longrightarrow W_{m_2}(M)</math> are birationally equivalent, which means there are the birational map <math>\varphi:W_{m_1}\longrightarrow W_{m_2}(M)</math>. Namely, the diagram depicted in the right figure is commutative.

Furthermore, one can select <math>M^*</math> that is birational with <math>M</math> and <math>W^*</math> that is birational with both <math>W_{m_1}</math> and <math>W_{m_1}</math> such that
:: <math>\Phi : M^* \longrightarrow W^* </math>
is birational map, the fibers of <math>\Phi</math> are simply connected and the general fibers of <math>\Phi</math>
:: <math>M^*_w:= \Phi^{-1}(w),\ \ w\in W^*</math>
have Kodaira dimension 0.

The above fiber structure is called the '''Iitaka fiber space.''' In the case of the surface S (''n'' = 2 = dim(S)), W<sup>*</sup> is the [[algebraic curve]], the fiber structure is of dimension 1, and then the general fibers have the Kodaira dimension 0 i.e. elliptic curve. Therefore, S is the elliptic surface. These fact can be generalized to the general ''n''. Therefore The study of the higher-dimensional birational geometry decompose to the part of κ=-∞,0,n and the fiber space whose fibers is of κ=0.

The following additional formula by Iitaka, called '''Iitaka conjecture''', is important for the classification of algebraic varieties or compact complex manifolds.

{{math_theorem|name=Iitaka　Conjecture|Let <math>f:V\rightarrow W</math> to be the fiber space from m-dimensional variety <math>V</math> to n-dimensional variety <math>W</math> and each fibers <math>V_w=f^{-1}(w)</math> connected. Then
:<math>\kappa(V)\ge\kappa(V_w)+\kappa(W).</math>}}

This conjecture has been only partly solved, for example in the case of 
[[Moishezon manifold]]s. The classification theory might been said to be the effort to solve the Iitaka conjecture and lead another theorems that the three-dimensional variety V is [[Abelian variety|abelian]] if and only if κ(V)=0 and q(V)=3 and its generalization so on. The [[minimal model program]] might be led from this conjecture.
